KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 1:30 PM EST...High pressure centered to 
the south of our region and large-scale upper ridging are 
leading to yet another tranquil weather day with just some 
passing high clouds. Temperatures were running a couple degrees 
higher than the previous forecast given mainly clear skies. 
Tonight, some additional mid and high clouds are likely for 
northern areas as a weak disturbance aloft tracks overhead, 
which will help to keep temperatures a few degrees warmer than 
the last couple nights. Areas further south and east see more 
breaks of clearing, which should allow lows dip into the 30s.

Tomorrow, the sfc high slides off to the east, while a warm front 
associated with a developing low in the Plains lifts north through 
the region. Moisture doesn't look overly impressive, and the best 
forcing remains N/NW of the region, but some light showers are 
possible across the southern ADKs tomorrow where there could be some 
southerly upslope enhancement. Rainfall amounts look to only be on 
the order of a few hundredths of an inch. For the rest of the 
region, another mainly dry day is expected. Some patchy fog will be 
possible tomorrow night as dew points rise. Tomorrow night will be 
warmer as well, with lows only in the 40s. Wednesday will be the 
warmest day this week as the upper ridge axis moves overhead. Highs 
will be in the upper 60s to low 70s, which is well above normal. It 
will also be more breezy (wind gusts up to 10-15 kt), especially in 
the N/S oriented valleys. Dew points continue to creep up with 
southerly flow. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Thursday, aforementioned sfc low becomes occluded as 
it tracks into the western Great Lakes region. PWATs rise to around 
1.5" ahead of the system's approaching occluded/cold front. We 
are still expecting showers to overspread the region from the 
west Thursday morning ahead of the cold front. Western areas, 
(especially the ADKs) have the best chance (60-70%) to see over 
a half inch of rain. However, 12z guidance this morning seems to
be catching onto a trend for these showers to weaken as they 
track eastwards through the region Thursday due to the cold
front outrunning the better upper-level forcing and dynamics. 
Accordingly, we have trended PoPs and QPF down slightly from the
previous forecast for southeastern portions of our CWA. Here, 
rainfall amounts Thursday generally look to be under a quarter 
inch, and possibly closer to a tenth of an inch for the Mid 
Hudson Valley and southwestern New England. 

Thursday night into Friday, the front will slow down and stall near 
or just east of our region. At the same time, the parent upper 
trough will phase with a northern stream feature digging into the 
Great Lakes, and potentially with a southern stream shortwave 
ejecting eastwards from the 4 corners region. As these features 
phase and track eastwards, a wave of low pressure will develop along 
the stalled front and track somewhere off the New England coast. 
Latest guidance (and especially AI guidance) suggests that the 
steady precip associated with this coastal low likely remains just 
east of our area with less phasing between the northern and
southern stream features and an overall progressive/positively
tilted upper trough. However, there are some ensembles that 
have a cleaner phase (due to faster southern stream energy) and 
a low track closer to the coast. This would result in more
widespread rain across the region. While not the most likely 
outcome, this scenario certainly can't be ruled out. Given very
dry weather over the last 2 weeks, any rain will be quite 
beneficial with no concerns at all for hydro issues. Even if we 
don't see the steadier/heavier rain with the coastal low, 
scattered showers and cooler weather are still expected as the 
upper trough/upper low tracks overhead Friday into the weekend.
